the \ceckt\ is a knowledge engineering tool that allows medical doctors to easily represent and query temporal rules on thousands of physiological events.
\ceckd improves performance with respect to CEC and that it can be used to support the development of monitoring rules for diabetes patients.
the kd-tree cached Event Calculus (CECKD) improves scalability and reduces the time to answer queries with respect to the Cached Event Calculus ( CEC).

the following questions. How to represent monitoring rules in a way that is easily understandable for medical doctors? How to index thousands of events in a way that can be queried in a few milliseconds?
the development of a knowledge engineering approach to represent monitoring rules in the context of a Personal Health System.

the following questions: How can medical doctors easily represent and query their knowledge in a database to monitor a large number of time series? How can the performance of a query engine be improved when querying a large number of data points?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the kd-tree cached calculus is an effective way to index event calculus rules and it is able to handle large numbers of events, which is a key factor for the development of personal health systems.
\ceckd, the extension of the CEC to use kd-trees, is a promising tool for the representation of knowledge in the context of Personal Health Systems.
the \ceckt\ outperforms the CEC in all the experiments conducted in terms of performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have designed and implemented a new indexing scheme to improve the performance of the CEC.
\ceckd is capable to handle thousands of events, while the current state of art can only handle hundreds of events.

we are able to index a time series with thousands of events, and that the indexing approach allows to query the time series in a way that is simple for medical doctors, who do not need any technical background.

kd-trees can be used to index the events in the event calculus, thus enabling the representation of large time series and their efficient processing.
